clinicalPearls: The most common cutaneous (microcystic) lymphatic malformation, now classified as a superficial lymphatic malformation.
Presents as clusters of clear, translucent, thick-walled vesicles likened to frogspawn, often with haemorrhagic red-black vesicles when blood enters.
Commonly affects the proximal limbs, limb girdles, axillae, trunk and oral cavity or tongue.
Frequently connected to deeper, larger lymphatic cisterns beneath the skin, which explains the high recurrence after superficial treatment.
Prone to recurrent leakage of clear lymph, oozing, bleeding and secondary cellulitis.
Usually congenital or appearing in early childhood, though it can present later in life.
MRI helps define the depth of the deeper cisternal component before intervention.
Treatment options include sclerotherapy, ablative laser and excision of the deep component, but recurrences are common.
reference.pathophysiology: Lymphangioma circumscriptum is a superficial (microcystic) lymphatic malformation in which dilated lymphatic channels form thin-walled vesicles within the papillary dermis. These superficial cisterns typically communicate with larger, muscular-walled lymphatic cisterns in the deeper dermis and subcutis that are disconnected from the normal lymphatic system; rhythmic contraction of the deep cisterns transmits pressure to the surface vesicles. Failure to address the deep component underlies the characteristic recurrence. As with other lymphatic malformations, many lesions harbour somatic PIK3CA-pathway activation, and communication with dermal capillaries accounts for the intermittent haemorrhagic appearance.
additionalDifferentials: Herpes simplex or zoster with grouped vesicles
Acquired cutaneous lymphangiectasia from lymphatic obstruction
additionalInvestigations: Clinical and dermoscopic assessment showing lacunae and frogspawn-like vesicles
Skin biopsy showing dilated papillary dermal lymphatics
MRI to define the deep cisternal component and overall extent
PIK3CA mutation testing in selected cases
Assessment for secondary infection when the lesion is inflamed
redFlags: Recurrent cellulitis or sepsis arising within the malformation
Persistent lymph leakage with skin breakdown
New firm nodularity in longstanding lymphoedema, raising concern for lymphangiosarcoma
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign but chronic and notoriously recurrent after treatment unless the deep cisternal component is addressed. Complications are mainly recurrent infection, leakage and cosmetic concern.
pitfalls: Treating only the visible surface vesicles and ignoring the deep cisterns, which guarantees recurrence.
Misdiagnosing grouped haemorrhagic vesicles as herpes infection.
Underestimating the extent without MRI before surgery.
Overlooking recurrent cellulitis as a driver of long-term morbidity.
references: Reviews of superficial lymphatic malformations and their management
management: Complete surgical excision incorporating the deep dermal and subcutaneous cisterns as the most definitive treatment, since leaving them drives recurrence
Ablative options such as carbon dioxide laser, sclerotherapy or radiofrequency for superficial vesicles or where surgery is unsuitable
Prompt antibiotics for secondary cellulitis, with skin and wound care for chronic lymph leakage and oozing
Consider mTOR inhibition with sirolimus for extensive or recurrent PIK3CA-driven disease
Define the deep cisternal extent with MRI before intervention to plan complete treatment
Refer to a vascular anomalies service for multidisciplinary planning
Counsel on the benign but notoriously recurrent nature and the cosmetic implications
